hub.head_title: Clash of Clans Mechanics Explained — Loot, Shields, Matchmaking, AI
hub.description: How Clash of Clans actually works underneath: loot availability, shields and Village Guard, matchmaking, troop AI and pathing, war scoring, and the rules the game never spells out.
hub.summary: The rules the game does not print. Loot percentages, shield timers, why your Giants walked around the wall you built for them, how war matchmaking decides your opponent, and what the search screen is really doing while you press next. These are the pages that make every other page make sense.

faq.q: Do these mechanics change with updates?
faq.a: The systems described here are stable across years; the numbers attached to them are not. Supercell has adjusted loot percentages, shield durations and league bonuses many times, but the underlying rules, that collectors hold a larger stealable share than storages, that damage grants a shield, that troops pick the nearest valid target, have held throughout.

faq.q: Where should I start?
faq.a: If you are farming, read loot mechanics, then shields and Village Guard, then matchmaking. If your attacks keep failing, read troop targeting and AI, then walls and pathing, then funnelling, in that order.

entries.name: Loot mechanics
entries.h1: Loot Mechanics: How Much You Can Actually Steal
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Loot Mechanics — Collectors vs Storages
entries.description: How Clash of Clans decides how much gold, elixir and dark elixir is available in an attack: collector share versus storage share, Town Hall loot, the loot cart, and league bonuses.
entries.blurb: Why the loot preview says 340k when the defender has three million in the bank.
entries.summary: The number on the search screen is not the defender's bank balance. It is a calculated slice, and the slice is calculated very differently depending on where the resources are sitting. Understanding that one distinction is the single biggest jump in farming efficiency most players ever make.

quick.Applies to: Multiplayer attacks on the main village
quick.Key rule: A far larger share of collector loot is stealable than storage loot
quick.Also stealable: Town Hall contents, and the Clan Castle in some modes
quick.Not stealable: Loot already spent on an upgrade in progress

sections.body:
Every base you attack holds resources in two fundamentally different places, and the game treats them under different rules.

Collector loot lives in gold mines, elixir collectors and dark elixir drills. These buildings generate resources continuously and hold them until the owner taps to collect. A large proportion of whatever is sitting in them is available to you. This is why an inactive base is such a prize: the owner has not logged in to empty the collectors, so they are capped and full, and almost all of that is yours if you can destroy the buildings.

Storage loot lives in gold storages, elixir storages and the dark elixir storage. Only a modest percentage of what is in storage is available, and that percentage falls as the defender's Town Hall level rises relative to yours. A player sitting on three million gold is not offering you three million gold; they are offering you a fraction, and the loot preview shows you that fraction before you commit.

The practical consequence is that two bases showing the same loot preview can be worth wildly different amounts of effort. One has the loot spread across eight lightly defended collectors on the perimeter. The other has it locked in two storages behind the core. Same number, completely different attack.

The preview on the search screen tells you the total available, not where it is. Learning to guess the split at a glance is the core farming skill:

  • Collectors visibly full, gold piled high on the mines, drills glowing: most of that preview is surface loot. A cheap army takes it without ever touching a wall.
  • Collectors empty but a big preview number: the loot is in storages, in the core, behind defences. That is a real attack, and you need to decide whether the haul justifies the army.
  • Preview number close to your minimum: remember that you will not get one hundred per cent of it. Troops die, timers expire, buildings survive. Budget for taking sixty to eighty per cent of the preview on a good attack.

The other half of the calculation used to be what your army cost to train. It no longer is: troops are free and there is no training queue, so an attack has nothing to earn back before it turns a profit. What an attack still costs you is the search fee, a fixed gold charge per attack set by your Town Hall level, and your time. That makes the decision simpler than it used to be. Any base above your minimum is worth attacking, and the skill is entirely in setting the minimum and skipping quickly, as covered in the farming loop tutorial.

sections.h: Town Hall loot and the Town Hall snipe
sections.body:
The Town Hall itself holds a small stash of resources, and destroying it awards that stash plus a star plus, historically, a shield. This created the classic Town Hall snipe: find a base whose Town Hall sits outside the walls, drop one or two cheap troops on it, take the loot and the star, and walk away in thirty seconds.

Supercell has adjusted this repeatedly over the years, and modern versions of the game are much less generous to snipers than early ones were. The general shape survives, though: an exposed Town Hall is free value, and burying your own Town Hall inside your walls is basic self-defence. If you see a Town Hall sitting outside the wall on a base with full collectors, you are looking at one of the cheapest attacks in the game.

When your own village is attacked, a portion of what the attacker stole from you reappears in a loot cart on your map. Tapping it returns those resources to you for free. It is small, it is easy to miss behind a building, and it is pure profit.

The habit worth building: every single time you open the game, sweep the map for the cart before you do anything else. Over months, a player who always collects the cart is meaningfully ahead of one who does not, and it costs nothing but attention.

Stolen loot is not the only income from an attack. Winning an attack also pays a league bonus, a flat award of gold, elixir and dark elixir determined by the league you are currently in. Higher leagues pay dramatically more.

This is the counterweight to the classic advice to drop trophies for easier bases. Low leagues offer weak opposition and plentiful inactive bases but nearly no bonus; high leagues offer a bonus that can rival the stolen loot itself but demand an army that reliably wins. There is no universal correct answer, only a break-even point that depends on your win rate and how much skipping you will tolerate. The full trade-off is laid out in trophies and leagues.

Defence in Clash of Clans is not mainly about winning defences. It is about being unprofitable to attack. Three habits do most of the work:

  • Never log off rich. Loot committed to an upgrade cannot be stolen. Before you close the game, dump surplus into whatever upgrade you can afford, walls included. Walls are the perfect sink because they consume any amount at any time.
  • Collect your collectors, or do not. Full collectors are a magnet, but resources in collectors that you never collect are also resources you are not using. Collect and spend, in one motion.
  • Bury your storages. Storages on the perimeter are surface loot. Storages in separate walled compartments in the core force an attacker to commit a real army for each one. See base building principles.

An attacker who scouts you, sees empty storages and a maxed-out upgrade queue will press next, and pressing next is exactly what you want them to do.

tables.caption: How much a single attack can take from a village at each Town Hall level, and what the attacker pays to search. Percentages are of the defender's current storage contents.

faq.q: Why can I only steal a small part of someone's gold?
faq.a: Because storage loot is deliberately capped. Only a set percentage of what a defender holds in storages is available to an attacker, and that percentage shrinks further when the defender's Town Hall is lower than yours. Collector loot is not capped the same way, which is why inactive bases with full mines are far more profitable than active bases with fat storages.

faq.q: What is the loot cart?
faq.a: A cart that appears on your own village after you are attacked, holding a share of the resources the attacker took. Tapping it returns those resources to you at no cost. It is easy to overlook behind buildings, so check for it every time you log in.

faq.q: Is it better to farm collectors or storages?
faq.a: Collectors, most of the time, because a much larger share of collector loot is stealable and collectors are usually the easiest buildings on the map to reach. Commit to a storage attack only when the loot preview is large enough to justify a full army and the losses that come with going into the core.

entries.name: Shields and Village Guard
entries.h1: Shields and Village Guard Explained
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Shields and Village Guard — How They Really Work
entries.description: How shields are earned and broken in Clash of Clans, what Village Guard does, how attacking under a shield costs you time, and how farmers use the shield cycle deliberately.
entries.blurb: The timer that decides when you can be attacked, and how to use it on purpose.
entries.summary: A shield stops other players attacking your village. Village Guard does the same thing for a shorter window without the restrictions. Together they set the rhythm of the game: when you are safe, when you are exposed, and when your loot is at risk. Most players treat shields as something that happens to them. Efficient players treat them as a resource to spend.

quick.What a shield does: Prevents other players from attacking your village
quick.How you get one: Automatically, when an attacker does enough damage to your base
quick.Shield strength: Scales with the damage percentage the attacker achieved
quick.Village Guard: A shorter protected window with no attack penalty
quick.Cost of attacking: Attacking under a shield reduces its remaining time

sections.body:
You are awarded a shield when someone attacks your village and does enough damage. The more damage they do, the longer the shield: a scrape gives you nothing, a partial destruction gives you a short shield, and a full wipe gives you the longest one. The exact thresholds and durations are Supercell's to change and have moved several times over the years, but the shape is constant, more damage taken means more protection granted.

This produces a counterintuitive truth that trips up new players: losing a defence is not necessarily bad. If your storages are empty because you spent everything before logging off, an attacker who flattens your base has taken almost nothing from you and handed you hours of free, protected farming time. You have effectively traded trophies you did not need for safety you did.

Village Guard is a short protected period, typically measured in tens of minutes to a few hours, during which you cannot be attacked. It appears in several situations: after a shield expires, after certain attacks, and as a reward from various parts of the game.

The critical difference from a shield is that attacking during Village Guard does not consume it. Under a shield, going on the offensive costs you protection. Under Guard, it does not. That makes Guard the single best window in the game to farm aggressively: you can attack repeatedly, stack up loot, and remain untouchable while you do it.

The mistake almost everyone makes is letting Guard tick away while they are at work or asleep. Guard is only worth what you do with it. If you see Guard time on the clock, that is the moment to train an army and go.

You can attack while holding a shield, but it costs you. Each attack reduces the shield's remaining duration, and after a limited number of attacks the shield ends entirely. The game tells you this before you commit, with a warning on the attack button.

How to think about it: a shield is a stock of protected hours, and each attack spends some of that stock. Spend it deliberately. Three high-value attacks that fund a hero upgrade are a good use of a shield. Five aimless attacks that net you nothing and end your protection early are not.

  • Scout before you spend. If you are going to burn shield time, make it count. Skip harder and set a higher loot minimum than you would normally.
  • Empty your storages first. The instant your shield ends you are exposed. Enter that moment with nothing worth taking.
  • Watch the queue. There is no point ending your shield to gather loot you have nowhere to spend. Have upgrades ready to start.

Experienced farmers run a repeating loop rather than playing at random:

  1. Log in, collect the loot cart and the collectors.
  2. Immediately queue upgrades so storages sit low.
  3. Fill an army, which is instant and free, and attack through whatever shield or Guard time is available rather than hoarding it.
  4. Spend the returns before logging off, walls absorbing whatever is left over.
  5. Get attacked while offline, be worth almost nothing to the attacker, and receive a fresh shield for the trouble.

Run consistently, this converts the thing that feels like a punishment, being raided, into a scheduling tool. You are never protecting a pile of loot, because there is never a pile of loot to protect.

A note on purchased protection. Shields have historically been buyable with gems. Whether that is ever worth it depends entirely on what you are protecting. If your storages are full and a hero upgrade is one attack away, maybe. If you follow the cycle above, you will almost never need to, which is rather the point.

faq.q: Does attacking break my shield in Clash of Clans?
faq.a: Not immediately. Attacking while shielded reduces the shield's remaining time, and the shield ends after a limited number of attacks. Village Guard is different: attacking during Guard does not consume it at all, which makes Guard the best window to farm aggressively.

faq.q: Is losing a defence bad?
faq.a: Often it is actively good. If your storages are empty, an attacker who destroys your base takes almost nothing and you receive a shield in exchange. Farmers deliberately keep storages low precisely so that defeats cost them little and buy them protected time.

faq.q: What is the difference between a shield and Village Guard?
faq.a: Both prevent other players from attacking you. A shield is longer and is spent when you attack; Village Guard is shorter but is not consumed by attacking, so you can farm freely underneath it.

entries.name: Matchmaking and the search screen
entries.h1: Matchmaking and the Search Screen
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Matchmaking and the Search Screen
entries.description: How multiplayer matchmaking works in Clash of Clans: trophy-based opponent selection, what nexting costs, why you see the bases you see, and how to search efficiently.
entries.blurb: What the game is doing while you press next, and how to press it less.
entries.summary: Multiplayer matchmaking pairs you with an opponent based principally on trophies, not on Town Hall level, base strength or how much loot they are holding. That single fact explains most of what players find frustrating about searching, and points directly at how to search better.

quick.Not matched on: Town Hall level, hero levels, base layout quality
quick.Search cost: A small gold fee per skip, rising the longer you search
quick.Search widens: The longer the game looks, the further from your trophy range it goes
quick.You cannot: Search for a specific player or a specific resource

sections.body:
When you tap Attack, the game looks for a village near your trophy count that is currently attackable, meaning it is not shielded, not under Guard and not currently being attacked by someone else. It does not filter by Town Hall level, and it does not care whether the base is a maxed fortress or an abandoned wreck.

Everything downstream follows from this. If you have pushed trophies well beyond your base's actual strength, matchmaking will keep handing you bases that outclass your army, because trophies are the only thing it is matching on. Conversely, if you deliberately drop trophies, you will meet weaker, poorer opponents, more of whom have quit. This is the trophy-versus-loot trade-off in a single sentence, and it is explored properly in trophies and leagues.

Skipping a base charges a small gold fee, and that fee escalates the longer you keep skipping within a single search session. In pure resource terms it is trivial next to the loot you are hunting.

The real cost of nexting is time, and, if you are honest about it, attention. Twenty minutes of tapping next to find one good base is twenty minutes you did not spend doing anything else, and the tenth base looks a lot like the second when you have stopped paying attention. Search discipline matters more than search cost:

  • Set a number before you start. Decide your minimum acceptable loot before the first base appears, and hold to it. Deciding case by case is how you end up attacking a mediocre base out of impatience.
  • Train while you search. Never sit on the search screen with an empty queue. The army should always be cooking.
  • Judge in three seconds. Loot preview, collector state, Town Hall position. If it fails, next. Do not study bases you are not going to attack.

sections.h: Why the same bases keep appearing
sections.body:
Two reasons, usually. First, at unusual trophy ranges, or at odd hours in your region, the pool of attackable villages near your trophy count is genuinely small, so you cycle through it. Second, the search widens its range the longer it looks, which is why the twentieth base often looks nothing like the first.

If you are seeing the same handful of bases, you have two levers: move your trophy count to enter a different pool, or search at a different time of day when a different part of the world is online and unshielded.

It is worth being clear about the limits, because a lot of folk wisdom claims otherwise:

  • You cannot search for a specific resource. Dark elixir hunting is not a search filter; it is skipping until you find drills worth hitting.
  • You cannot search for a specific player or revenge someone who has not attacked you.
  • You cannot make inactive bases appear more often. They are simply villages in your trophy range whose owners stopped playing, and pushing into ranges those players occupied is the only lever you have.
  • Base layout quality is not a matchmaking input. A perfectly designed base and a random pile of buildings at the same trophy count are equally likely to be offered to you.

What you can control is your trophy range, the time you search, your loot minimum, and how quickly you make the skip-or-attack call. That is the whole game on the search screen.

faq.q: Does Town Hall level affect who I am matched against?
faq.a: Not for multiplayer matchmaking, which pairs you primarily on trophies. Town Hall level does affect how much storage loot is available to you when there is a mismatch, and it matters a great deal in war matchmaking, which uses an entirely different system.

faq.q: Does skipping bases cost anything?
faq.a: Yes, a small gold fee per skip that escalates during a long search session. It is negligible compared to the loot you are looking for. The genuine cost of nexting is your time.

faq.q: How do I find inactive bases?
faq.a: There is no filter for them. Inactive bases are simply villages in your trophy range whose owners quit, so the practical approach is to sit in a trophy range where more players have stopped playing and to skip quickly with a firm loot minimum.

entries.name: Trophies and leagues
entries.h1: Trophies and Leagues: The Farming Trade-off
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Trophies and Leagues — Pushing vs Farming
entries.description: How trophies and leagues work in Clash of Clans, what league bonuses pay, why farmers deliberately drop trophies, and how to decide where to sit.
entries.blurb: Why good players sometimes throw defences on purpose.
entries.summary: Trophies measure competitive standing and decide who you are matched against. Leagues, which are bands of trophy count, decide how large a bonus you collect for winning an attack. The two pull in opposite directions for anyone who cares about resources, and choosing where to sit is one of the few genuinely strategic decisions in the game.

quick.Trophies gained: By winning attacks, and by successfully defending
quick.Trophies lost: By losing attacks, and by being successfully attacked
quick.League: A band of trophy count, re-evaluated as you move
quick.League bonus: A flat resource award for winning an attack, larger in higher leagues
quick.Season reset: Trophies above a threshold are reduced at the end of a season

sections.body:
Trophies do two jobs. They are the game's ladder, so they determine your league and your standing. And they are the input to multiplayer matchmaking, so they determine who you meet, as covered in matchmaking and the search screen.

The second job is the one that matters for resources. Your trophy count is a dial that sets the difficulty and the wealth of the opponents the game offers you. Turn it up and you meet stronger, richer, more active players. Turn it down and you meet weaker, poorer, more frequently abandoned ones.

sections.h: The league bonus, and why it complicates everything
sections.body:
If leagues only gated matchmaking, the answer would be simple: drop as low as tolerable and farm inactive bases forever. But winning an attack also pays a league bonus, a flat award of gold, elixir and dark elixir that scales steeply with league. In the highest leagues, the bonus alone can be worth more than the loot you steal.

So the decision becomes an actual calculation:

  • Low leagues. Cheap opposition, many inactive bases with full collectors, minimal bonus. Income comes almost entirely from stolen collector loot. Works brilliantly with the cheapest possible armies, and tolerates a low win rate because you were not counting on the bonus anyway.
  • High leagues. Strong opposition, few inactive bases, large bonus per win. Income depends on winning, and since the army itself is free, what a failed attack costs you is the search fee and several minutes. Profitable only if your win rate is genuinely high.

The break-even sits wherever your win rate and your patience say it does, and it moves as your base grows. A player who can three-star reliably belongs higher than one who cannot, regardless of Town Hall level.

Dropping trophies on purpose, sometimes by dropping a single troop and quitting, is a long-established farming tactic. It works because it moves you into a matchmaking pool with more abandoned bases and cheaper opposition, and because trophies you are not using are not doing anything for you.

Some caveats worth knowing before you do it:

  • It is slow. Getting down takes many deliberate losses, and the game will keep handing you trophies for successful defences on the way.
  • It is reversible but tedious. Climbing back up costs real attacks.
  • It affects your clan. Some clans have trophy requirements, and low trophy counts can affect where you sit in clan listings.
  • It does not help war. War matchmaking does not use trophies, so dropping does nothing for your war matchups.

sections.h: Season resets and where to settle
sections.body:
At the end of each competitive season, trophy counts above a threshold are pulled back down, and rewards are handed out based on the league you finished in. This mostly concerns players near the top of the ladder; if you are farming in the middle, resets barely register.

For everyone else, the practical advice is boring and correct: settle at the highest league where you still win comfortably with a cheap army. If you are skipping endlessly because nothing has loot, move up. If your cheap army keeps failing against real defences, move down. Test it deliberately for a week rather than guessing, and let the actual loot per hour decide.

sections.h: Why there is no league table on this page
sections.body:
Every other stat table on this wiki is read from Clash of Clans' own game files. League trophy thresholds and bonus values are not in the files we read, so publishing a table of them would mean transcribing numbers from somewhere else and presenting them with the same confidence as the verified ones.

We would rather say that plainly. The trade-off described above does not depend on the exact figures, and the current bonus for your league is shown in game on the league badge, which is both authoritative and up to date.

faq.q: Should I drop trophies to farm?
faq.a: Only if you are struggling to find profitable bases where you are. Dropping puts you among weaker, poorer, more frequently abandoned opponents, which suits very cheap armies. It also costs you the league bonus, which in higher leagues can exceed the loot you steal, so it is a trade rather than a free win.

faq.q: What is the best league for farming?
faq.a: The highest one where a cheap army still wins comfortably. That is a different league for different players and it changes as your base grows, so test it: farm a week in one league, a week in the next, and compare actual resources gained per hour rather than trusting a rule of thumb.

faq.q: Do trophies affect clan war matchmaking?
faq.a: No. War matchmaking uses an entirely separate system based on the composition and strength of the participating rosters, so trophy dropping has no effect on the wars your clan is given.

entries.name: Troop targeting and AI
entries.h1: Troop Targeting and AI: Why Your Troops Do That
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Troop AI and Targeting Explained
entries.description: How Clash of Clans troops choose targets: preferred targets, nearest-target logic, air versus ground, and why your Giants ignored the cannon right next to them.
entries.blurb: Nearest valid target, every time, with a short list of exceptions.
entries.summary: Clash of Clans troops are not clever. They follow a small set of rules with total consistency, and almost every attack that fails does so because the attacker expected intelligence where there was only a rule. Learn the rules and you stop being surprised.

quick.Default behaviour: Move to and attack the nearest valid target
quick.Preferred targets: Some troops ignore the default in favour of a building type
quick.When preferred targets are gone: The troop reverts to nearest-target behaviour
quick.Air and ground: Ground troops walk and are blocked by walls; air troops fly over everything
quick.Defending troops: Clan Castle troops and heroes actively chase attackers

sections.body:
Unless a troop has a preferred target, it walks toward whatever building is closest to it and attacks that. Not the most dangerous building. Not the building you want it to attack. The closest one.

This is why deployment position is the most important decision in an attack. A troop dropped at the corner of a base will attack the corner. A troop dropped next to a wall with a storage on the other side will, more often than not, walk around the wall to reach a building that is easier to get to, because it is looking for a path to the nearest target and the wall is not on the way.

Everything else in this page is an exception to this rule.

Some troops ignore nearest-target logic and instead seek out one category of building, walking past everything else to reach it, taking damage the entire way. These are the units that make or break attacks:

  • Giants prefer defences. They will march past storages and huts to reach a cannon.
  • Goblins prefer resource buildings, and deal bonus damage to them. Dropped in the wrong place they sprint into the core after a storage and die.
  • Wall Breakers prefer walls, specifically walls that protect something they have not yet reached.
  • Hog Riders prefer defences and jump walls rather than breaking them.
  • Balloons prefer defences, from the air.
  • Miners travel underground and are untargetable while doing so.

The critical corollary: once every building of a troop's preferred type is destroyed, it reverts to plain nearest-target behaviour. Giants that have flattened every defence will happily wander off to punch a builder's hut on the far side of the map while the timer runs out. This single behaviour is responsible for an enormous number of failed 99% attacks.

The other hard division is movement type. Ground troops walk, are stopped by walls, and can be hit by every defence except pure anti-air. Air troops fly in a straight line over walls, buildings and traps, and can only be hit by defences that target air.

Two practical consequences. First, walls are worth nothing against air; a base with beautiful compartments and one Air Defence is a free win for Dragons. Second, air attacks are far more predictable, because you have removed pathing from the equation entirely, which is exactly why they are the standard recommendation for newer players.

A handful of troops sit in between: some ground units jump walls, some travel underground, and some switch behaviour when damaged. Those exceptions are noted on each unit's own page.

Most of the base is passive: buildings sit still and shoot whatever comes near. Three things are not passive, and they will come to you.

  • Clan Castle troops deploy when an attacker enters their radius and then chase, aggressively and across the whole map. Dealing with them is a skill of its own, covered in Clan Castle troops.
  • Defending heroes wake up when an attacker comes within range of their altar and then fight like a troop, pursuing targets.
  • Skeleton and similar traps spawn units that behave like troops rather than dealing instant damage.

The pattern for all three is the same: pull them out to somewhere harmless, kill them there, then attack the base you actually wanted to attack. An attack that walks into a defending Castle with the main army is an attack that has already gone wrong.

Once you accept that troops are simple, you can steer them:

  • Clear the outside first. Ground troops only path inward when there is nothing left outside. Destroying the perimeter buildings on a side is what forces the army in, and it is the whole idea behind funnelling.
  • Deploy in a line, not a pile. Troops dropped on top of each other die to a single splash defence. Spread along a side, they engage more buildings and survive longer.
  • Send the tank first. Whatever soaks damage goes down several seconds before whatever deals it, so the defences are already busy when the fragile units arrive.
  • Watch for the revert. When the last defence falls and your Giants pause, that is the moment to drop clean-up troops on the buildings you still need, because the Giants are about to wander.

faq.q: Why do my Giants ignore the nearby cannon?
faq.a: They are not ignoring it, they are pathing to the nearest defence they can actually reach. If a wall blocks the direct route, the game routes them around it toward whichever defence has a walkable path, which is frequently not the one you had in mind. Break the wall, or deploy where the route you want is the shortest one.

faq.q: Do troops attack walls?
faq.a: Only when a wall blocks the path to their target and going around would take significantly longer, or when the troop is a Wall Breaker, which targets walls deliberately. Most ground troops prefer to walk around, which is why wall compartments funnel attacks rather than stopping them.

faq.q: What happens when all the defences are destroyed?
faq.a: Troops with a defence preference revert to normal nearest-target behaviour and start attacking whatever building is closest, including huts and decorations at the far edge of the map. This is a common cause of failed attacks that end at 99 per cent with the timer expired.

entries.name: Walls and pathing
entries.h1: Walls and Pathing: What Walls Actually Do
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Walls and Pathing Explained
entries.description: How walls affect troop pathing in Clash of Clans: why walls redirect rather than stop, what compartments achieve, and how attackers get through them.
entries.blurb: Walls do not stop troops. They redirect them, which is more useful.
entries.summary: New players build walls to keep troops out. Walls do not keep troops out. They make troops take a longer route, and that longer route is spent under fire. Understanding walls as a delay-and-redirect tool rather than a barrier changes how you build and how you attack.

quick.Effect on ground troops: Blocks direct movement, forcing a longer path
quick.Broken by: Wall Breakers, and by troops that choose to attack the wall
quick.Ignored by: Wall-jumping troops, tunnelling troops, and Jump Spells
quick.Upgrade cost: Consumes gold and elixir in very large quantities

sections.body:
When a ground troop wants to reach a target and a wall is in the way, the game evaluates whether walking around is cheaper than breaking through. Usually it is, so the troop walks around. That is the entire mechanic, and it is far more useful to a defender than an impassable barrier would be.

A troop walking around your wall is a troop spending several extra seconds inside the range of your defences, not attacking anything, taking damage. Time is the resource walls take away from an attacker. A wall that adds four seconds to every troop's route across a base defended by four splash defences has done more work than a wall that stops a single Giant.

sections.h: Compartments are the real design unit
sections.body:
A single ring of wall around everything is close to worthless: attackers break one segment and the entire interior is open. What matters is compartmentalisation, dividing the interior into many small walled cells so that breaking in gives access to one building, not the whole base.

  • Every compartment breached is a separate decision for the attacker, and separate Wall Breakers, and separate time.
  • Storages make excellent compartment walls because they have large hitpoints and are worth taking, so they slow troops that stop to attack them.
  • Do not double-wall. Two wall segments side by side cost twice as much and are broken by the same charge. Use the saved segments to add another compartment instead.
  • Leave no gaps. A single missing segment is a door, and pathing will find it instantly. Check your layout for one-tile openings, especially where a building was moved.

More layout theory lives in base building principles.

Four methods, in rough order of cost:

  1. Walk around. Free. Works whenever the base has an easier route, which most badly designed bases do.
  2. Wall Breakers. Cheap, fragile, and targeted specifically at walls that protect something new. A handful turns a surface attack into a core attack. They die instantly to splash damage, so they go in behind a tank.
  3. Jump over. Hog Riders jump walls natively; a Jump Spell creates a temporary crossing for any ground troop. Both convert a compartment maze into open ground, which is exactly why heavily compartmented bases are vulnerable to hog-based attacks.
  4. Go under or over. Miners tunnel and ignore walls entirely; every air troop ignores them by definition.

The design conclusion for defenders is that walls must be part of a system. A base compartmented to defeat Giants is a base that Hog Riders find comfortable; a base built to defeat air is a base with more anti-air than walls. You cannot be strong against everything, and choosing what to be weak to is what base design is.

Walls are the most expensive thing in the game by total cost, and there is no research, no builder occupied, and no timer. You tap, you pay, it is instantly upgraded.

That makes walls the perfect place to dump surplus. Any gold or elixir left over when you log off should go into walls, because loot in a wall cannot be stolen and loot in a storage can. Do not, however, prioritise walls over defences or heroes. Walls buy you seconds; a missing Air Defence loses you the whole base. Walls are what you do with money you have nowhere better to put, which, at most stages of the game, is a lot of money.

Practical rule. Upgrade walls from the outside in and from the core out at the same time, meeting in the middle, rather than doing one ring at a time. Mixed wall levels are ugly but functionally fine; a fully upgraded outer ring around an unupgraded core is not.

faq.q: Do walls actually stop troops in Clash of Clans?
faq.a: No. Walls block direct movement, so ground troops path around them unless breaking through is genuinely faster. The value of a wall is the extra seconds an attacker spends walking under fire, not any ability to keep troops out.

faq.q: Should I double-wall my base?
faq.a: No. Two adjacent wall segments cost double and are opened by the same Wall Breaker charge. Spend those segments on additional compartments instead, which forces the attacker to make and pay for more separate breaches.

faq.q: Are walls worth upgrading?
faq.a: Yes, but never before defences, heroes or army research. Walls are instant, need no builder and accept unlimited amounts of loot, which makes them the ideal place to spend surplus resources you would otherwise leave sitting in a storage where they can be stolen.

entries.name: Clan Castle troops
entries.h1: Clan Castle Troops: Donations, Luring and Defending
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Clan Castle — Donations and Luring
entries.description: How the Clan Castle works in Clash of Clans: requesting and donating troops, defensive Clan Castle behaviour, and how to lure and kill a defending Castle.
entries.blurb: The one part of a base that fights back and follows you home.
entries.summary: The Clan Castle is the only building that puts an active, mobile opponent on the field. On offence it is free reinforcement from your clanmates. On defence it is the single most disruptive thing in a base. Handling it, in both directions, separates players who win attacks from players who nearly win attacks.

quick.Offensive use: Carries donated troops, spells and siege machines into your attacks
quick.Defensive use: Deploys its troops automatically when an attacker enters its radius
quick.Trigger: Proximity, the radius is larger than most players expect
quick.Behaviour once out: Actively chases attacking troops anywhere on the map
quick.Refill: By clan donation only, and it is not automatic

sections.h: Donations, and why they matter more than they look
sections.body:
Members request troops in clan chat and other members fill the request. The donor pays nothing meaningful and gains clan XP and donation credit; the receiver gets troops they may not even have unlocked, for free.

For a new player this is enormous. A Town Hall 5 player in a good clan can carry a Dragon into every attack. It is the fastest legitimate power boost in the game, and it costs nothing but being in a clan that donates.

  • Ask specifically. Type what you want and why. "Any troops" gets you whatever someone had spare, which is usually the cheapest thing they had spare.
  • Donate back. Most clans track ratios, and the clans worth being in remove people who only take. Donating is also how you get clan XP.
  • Keep a separate defensive request. The troops you want defending your base are not the ones you want attacking with, and swapping between them is a normal part of play.

When an attacker's troops come within the Castle's radius, the garrison deploys and immediately goes hunting. It does not defend a position; it chases. A single strong defensive Castle troop can eat an entire wave of fragile attackers before it dies.

What makes it so disruptive is that the radius is generous and the trigger is invisible until it fires. Attackers who deploy their main army along a side, expecting a clean run, frequently discover the Castle mid-attack, at which point their army is committed and scattered and the Castle is already among them.

What to put in your own Castle, in general terms: something with high hitpoints that survives long enough to matter, or something with splash damage that punishes massed cheap troops. What not to put in it: anything fragile, and anything that dies to a single spell. Clans usually have a house preference; ask.

sections.h: Luring: the routine that wins attacks
sections.body:
The counter to a defensive Castle is always the same four-step routine, and it should become automatic:

  1. Find the radius.Drop a single cheap troop near the edge of the base, one tile at a time, until the Castle fires. One Barbarian is enough. This costs you almost nothing and tells you everything.
  2. Pull them out.Once the garrison is out and chasing, drop another cheap troop far from the base, in open ground or at a corner. Defending troops chase, so they will come to it.
  3. Kill them there.Away from the base, away from the defences, surround them with cheap troops or drop a spell on the clump. Killing a Castle in open ground costs a fraction of what killing it inside the base costs.
  4. Then attack.Only now do you deploy the army you actually planned. The base is now passive, apart from heroes.

Skipping the lure to save ninety seconds is the most common self-inflicted defeat in the game. The lure is not optional; it is part of the attack.

In Clan Wars the Castle matters more than anywhere else, because war bases are designed around it. A war Castle is typically filled with the strongest defensive troops the clan can donate, and its radius is deliberately positioned so that it covers the approaches an attacker would naturally take.

Two war-specific habits:

  • Scout the Castle before planning. The war map shows whether a Castle is filled. Plan the lure before you plan the attack, not after.
  • Fill your own, early. An empty war Castle on defence is a free star for the enemy. Request as soon as war starts, not five minutes before battle day ends.

More on war structure in Clan Wars.

faq.q: How do I lure Clan Castle troops?
faq.a: Drop one cheap troop near the base edge to find the Castle's trigger radius, then, once the garrison deploys, drop another cheap troop well away from the base. Defending troops chase, so they will follow it into open ground where you can kill them cheaply before starting your real attack.

faq.q: What is the best troop to put in a defensive Clan Castle?
faq.a: Something durable enough to survive a lure attempt, or something with splash damage that punishes the clumps of cheap troops attackers use to bait it. Fragile single-target troops die instantly and give the attacker a free run. Most clans have a preferred defensive donation, so ask before guessing.

faq.q: Do Clan Castle troops chase attackers?
faq.a: Yes, aggressively and across the entire map. That is precisely why luring works: you can pull the garrison far from the base's defences and kill it somewhere it gets no support.

entries.name: Spell mechanics
entries.h1: Spell Mechanics: Radius, Timing and Stacking
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Spell Mechanics — Radius, Timing, Stacking
entries.description: How spells work in Clash of Clans: area of effect, duration, whether spells stack, dark versus regular spell factory, and when to drop each type.
entries.blurb: Where you drop it and when matters more than which one you brought.
entries.summary: Spells are the smallest part of an army by housing space and the largest part by outcome. A correctly timed Rage turns a stalled push into a three-star; the same spell dropped four seconds early does nothing at all. The mechanics that govern them are simple, and almost nobody reads them.

quick.Two factories: Spell Factory for regular spells, Dark Spell Factory for dark spells
quick.Housing: Spells occupy separate spell housing, not troop housing
quick.Area of effect: Circular, centred where you tap, fixed radius per spell
quick.Duration: Timed, and the timer starts the moment it lands
quick.Stacking: Most same-type effects do not stack usefully; overlapping radii extend coverage, not power

sections.body:
Regular spells come from the Spell Factory and are paid for in elixir. Dark spells come from the Dark Spell Factory and are paid for in dark elixir. They share the same spell housing space, but dark spells occupy less of it, which is why a mixed set is usually better value than a pure one.

Broadly, regular spells do the big, expensive things: mass healing, mass damage boosts, opening walls, freezing defences. Dark spells do the small, cheap, surgical things: poisoning defending troops, disabling a single defence, speeding up a push, spawning a distraction. A well-built army usually carries a couple of large regular spells and one or two cheap dark ones for a specific job.

Every spell affects a circle centred exactly where you tap, with a fixed radius. Three consequences that decide most attacks:

  • Drop ahead of the army, not on it. Troops move. A Rage centred on your troops right now is centred behind them two seconds from now. Aim where the front of the push will be.
  • Cover the group, not the star player. A spell that covers eight troops is worth four times one that covers two. If the army has spread out, the spell is already partly wasted, which is another reason to deploy in a controlled line.
  • Overlapping does not multiply. Two Rage spells on the same troops do not double the effect. Overlapping is for extending the covered area or the duration, when a push must cross a long stretch of base.

The duration clock starts on impact, not on first effect, so a spell dropped before the troops arrive is a spell partly spent on empty ground. The general timing rules:

  • Rage goes down when the troops are already engaged with something worth killing quickly, not while they are walking.
  • Heal goes down when the damage is already happening, ideally where the army will remain for the full duration. Healing a group that is about to walk out of the circle wastes most of it.
  • Freeze is reactive, not planned. You hold it for the moment a specific defence starts shredding your army, most often an Inferno Tower or a Scattershot, and you drop it then.
  • Jump goes down before the troops reach the wall, because it takes a moment to open and the army does not wait.
  • Poison goes on defending Clan Castle troops as soon as they are clumped, during the lure, not during the main attack.

The habit that improves attacks fastest: hold your spells. New players dump every spell in the first fifteen seconds because it feels productive. Attacks are lost at the sixty-second mark, and that is when the spells should still be in your hand.

Work backwards from the failure mode of your army, not forwards from a list.

  • If the army dies to splash damage, bring healing.
  • If the army survives but runs out of time, bring haste or rage.
  • If the army stalls at a specific defence every time, bring the counter to that defence, usually freeze.
  • If the army cannot get into the core, bring jump or more wall breakers.
  • If the army dies to the defending Castle, bring poison and lure properly.

Then, and this is the part people skip, watch the replay of the attack that failed and check which of those five it actually was. The right spell is a diagnostic result, not a preference.

faq.q: Do spells stack in Clash of Clans?
faq.a: Not usefully in terms of power. Two of the same spell on the same troops do not double the effect. What overlapping achieves is a larger covered area or a longer covered window, which is what you want when a push has to travel across a wide base.

faq.q: When should I drop a Rage spell?
faq.a: When the troops are already engaged and the extra damage will land on something that matters, and slightly ahead of them so they move into the circle rather than out of it. Rage dropped while an army is walking across open ground is mostly wasted.

faq.q: Are dark spells better than regular spells?
faq.a: They are different tools. Dark spells cost dark elixir and take less spell housing, which suits cheap, surgical jobs such as poisoning a defending Castle. Regular spells do the heavy lifting. Most strong armies carry a mix rather than committing to one factory.

entries.name: Funnelling
entries.h1: Funnelling: Steering an Army Into the Core
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Funnelling Explained — How to Steer Your Army
entries.description: What funnelling means in Clash of Clans, why armies drift around the outside of a base, and how to build a funnel so your main force goes through the core.
entries.blurb: The single technique that separates 50 per cent attacks from three stars.
entries.summary: Funnelling is the practice of destroying specific outside buildings before the main army goes in, so that the path of least resistance runs through the middle of the base rather than around its edge. It is not an advanced trick. It is the basic requirement for any ground attack, and skipping it is why most attacks stall.

quick.Problem it solves: Ground troops walking around the base instead of into it
quick.Cause of the problem: Nearest-target pathing plus buildings on the outside
quick.How it works: Clear the outside buildings on two sides so the only nearby targets are inward
quick.Cost: A small share of the army, spent deliberately
quick.Applies to: Every ground attack, and most mixed attacks

sections.body:
Ground troops go to the nearest reachable target. On a typical base, the nearest reachable targets from any deployment point are the outside buildings: army camps, huts, collectors, a spare barracks. So the army eats the outside of the base, working its way around the ring, while the timer runs and the core sits untouched.

You have seen the result: 51 per cent, two stars, every defence in the middle still standing. The army did not fail. It did exactly what it was told, which was nothing, because nobody told it anything.

A funnel is a cleared corridor. You destroy the outside buildings on either side of your intended entry point, so that when the main army lands, the closest remaining targets are inward, and the pathing carries the whole force into the core together.

  1. Pick your side.Choose the approach with the fewest outside buildings to clear and, ideally, the most valuable defences on the way in. Look at the base for five seconds before you deploy anything, every time.
  2. Clear the shoulders.Use a small, cheap portion of the army, or a hero, to destroy the outside buildings to the left and right of the entry point. Not the whole side, just the shoulders of the corridor.
  3. Check the gap.Before committing, confirm there is nothing left outside on those two flanks that could pull troops sideways. A single surviving hut ruins a funnel.
  4. Send the main army into the gap.Deploy in a controlled line at the mouth of the corridor, tank first, damage behind, and it will go inward because inward is now nearest.
  5. Support with spells.Once the force is engaged in the core, spells go down. Not before.

Whatever you can afford to lose. The classic tools:

  • Heroes. The Barbarian King and Archer Queen are excellent funnellers because they are durable, hit hard, and you get them back after the attack. Sending a hero down each shoulder is the standard opening for a great many attacks.
  • A handful of cheap troops. A few Barbarians or Archers per side, dropped on the outside buildings, does the job for almost nothing.
  • One or two heavy units. A Baby Dragon or similar on each flank clears the shoulders quickly and keeps up with the main push afterwards.

What you should not funnel with is your main damage. If you send the whole army in to clear the outside, you have not funnelled, you have just attacked the outside.

Two cases. Pure air attacks care much less, because air troops fly straight over the buildings that would have distracted a ground army; they still drift toward the nearest target, but the geometry is far more predictable. And farming attacks on inactive bases often do not need a funnel at all, because you are not trying to reach the core, you are trying to strip the collectors on the outside, which is where the army wants to go anyway.

That second case is worth stating plainly, because it is a real distinction between farming and war. In farming, the army drifting to the outside is frequently exactly what you want. In war, it is the thing that costs you the star.

faq.q: What does funnelling mean in Clash of Clans?
faq.a: Destroying selected buildings on the outside of a base before committing your main army, so that the nearest remaining targets lead inward and the army paths into the core instead of wandering around the perimeter.

faq.q: Do I need to funnel for every attack?
faq.a: For essentially every ground attack in war, yes. For farming attacks aimed at collectors on the outside of an inactive base, usually not, because the outside is where you want the troops to go anyway.

faq.q: What should I use to funnel?
faq.a: Heroes first, because they are durable and you get them back, then a small number of cheap troops. Never use your main damage dealers to clear the outside; the point of the funnel is to preserve the main army for the core.

entries.name: Siege machines
entries.h1: Siege Machines: Getting Your Army Into the Core
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Siege Machines — What They Do and When to Use Them
entries.description: How siege machines work in Clash of Clans: what they carry, how they deliver Clan Castle troops into a base, and how to choose between the wall-breaking and flying options.
entries.blurb: The delivery vehicle for your Clan Castle troops, and a funnel on wheels.
entries.summary: A siege machine is not really a troop. It is a delivery system: it carries your Clan Castle troops toward the middle of the base and releases them there, solving the oldest problem in attacking, which is that the good troops arrive at the core already dead. Choosing one is choosing how you want to get in.

quick.Unlocked by: The Workshop, at a mid-game Town Hall
quick.Carries: Your Clan Castle troops into the attack
quick.Used from: The Clan Castle slot in the army screen
quick.If it dies early: The Castle troops deploy on the spot
quick.Donatable: Yes, clanmates can donate siege machines

sections.body:
Before siege machines existed, Clan Castle troops walked in with everything else, which meant they spent the first half of the attack on the outside of the base fighting huts, and arrived at the core with a fraction of their health. Your best donated troops did their least useful work.

A siege machine changes that. It moves toward the centre under its own power, absorbing damage on the way, and releases the Castle troops when it arrives or when it dies. In effect you are teleporting your reinforcements past the boring part of the base.

The secondary benefit is just as valuable: while the siege machine is rolling in, it is destroying buildings and eating defence fire, which does a great deal of funnelling work for free.

Every siege machine is one of two things, and the choice is really about what your army needs.

  • Ground siege that breaks through. Rolls toward the core, smashing walls and buildings in a straight line. Creates a physical corridor that the rest of your ground army follows. Vulnerable to being destroyed early by concentrated defence fire, in which case the Castle troops pop out wherever it fell.
  • Flying siege that goes over. Ignores walls entirely and drops the Castle troops in the middle. Cannot be stopped by layout, only by anti-air. Delivers reinforcements precisely but does not open a path for your ground army.

There are also siege options that behave more like static support, sitting where deployed and providing continuous value rather than travelling. Each machine's own page covers the specifics; the strategic choice is nearly always corridor versus delivery.

Work from the base you are looking at, not from habit:

  • Heavily compartmented base, ground army. Take the breaker. You need a corridor, and walking your army around three wall layers is how attacks time out.
  • Open base, or an air army. Take the flier. There is nothing to break through; you want the Castle troops in the middle immediately.
  • Strong anti-air, ground army. Take the breaker. A flier that dies over the outer ring has delivered nothing.
  • Anti-ground core with heavy splash. Take the flier. A ground siege parked in front of a Scattershot is a very expensive firework.

• Deploying it last. The siege should usually go early, so it is soaking damage and clearing a route while the army follows, not arriving after the army has already died.
  • Deploying it into the strongest side. It is durable, not invincible. Send it in where the defences are thinnest, and let the corridor it opens dictate where the rest of the army goes.
  • Forgetting what is inside it. The siege machine is only as good as the Castle troops it is carrying. An empty Castle in a siege machine is a very slow wall breaker.
  • Not requesting one. Siege machines are donatable. If you have not unlocked the Workshop yet, ask.

faq.q: What happens if my siege machine is destroyed before it reaches the core?
faq.a: The Clan Castle troops it was carrying deploy immediately at the point where it was destroyed. You do not lose them, but you lose the delivery, so they arrive wherever the machine happened to die rather than where you wanted them.

faq.q: Do I need a siege machine for every attack?
faq.a: For war attacks, almost always, because getting Castle troops into the core at full health is worth far more than anything else you could put in that slot. For cheap farming attacks on collectors, usually not.

faq.q: Can siege machines be donated?
faq.a: Yes. Clanmates can donate siege machines the same way they donate troops, which means you can use one before you have built the Workshop yourself.

entries.name: Defence mechanics
entries.h1: Defence Mechanics: Splash, Single Target, Air and Ground
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Defences — Splash vs Single Target
entries.description: How defences work in Clash of Clans: single-target versus splash damage, air and ground targeting, range and blind spots, and how to build a balanced defensive set.
entries.blurb: What each category of defence is for, and what it cannot touch.
entries.summary: Every defence in the game sits somewhere on two axes: what it can shoot at, and whether it hits one thing hard or many things a little. A base that is strong on one axis and empty on the other is not a strong base, it is a base with an obvious answer, and every attacker will find it.

quick.Axis one: Targets ground only, air only, or both
quick.Axis two: Single-target damage, or splash damage over an area
quick.Range: Fixed per defence, and some have a minimum range or blind spot
quick.Priority: Defences fire at whatever enters range, with per-building rules
quick.Key weakness: Any base missing one whole category has a free counter

sections.body:
Single-target defences pick one unit and shoot it until it dies. They deal high damage per shot and are the correct answer to a small number of large, expensive units: a Golem, a hero, a Dragon. They are close to useless against thirty Barbarians, because they kill one at a time while the other twenty-nine chew through the building.

Splash defences deal damage over an area. Each individual hit is weaker, but it lands on everything in the circle. They are the correct answer to masses of cheap troops, and they are what makes swarm strategies fail. Against a single Golem, they are a rounding error.

This is the entire defensive balance problem in one line: you need both, because the attacker chooses which one you will face. A base packed with single-target defences dies to swarms. A base packed with splash dies to a handful of heavy units. The attacker gets to look at your base before deciding, so any hole you leave is the hole they will attack through.

The second axis is targeting. Ground-only defences cannot touch a single air unit; air-only defences cannot touch a single ground unit; some defences hit both.

The failure mode here is more common and more brutal than the splash one, because air attacks are the default recommendation for newer players. A base with one Air Defence, however well compartmented, is a base that Dragons walk through, and walls contribute exactly nothing to stopping them. Conversely, a base that over-invests in anti-air while leaving thin ground coverage gets flattened by hogs and miners.

Rule of thumb for placement: anti-air belongs deep, spread apart, and never all on one side. Air Defences clustered together die to one Rage and a stack of Balloons; spread across the base, each one has to be dealt with separately.

Each defence has a fixed range, drawn as a circle when you tap it in edit mode. Two things matter about those circles:

  • Overlap is the point. A defence standing alone gets destroyed alone. Defences whose circles overlap cover each other, so an attacker who commits to one is being shot by three. Layout is really the art of arranging overlapping circles.
  • Some defences have a minimum range. The Mortar is the classic example: it cannot hit anything standing directly on top of it. Attackers exploit this deliberately, and defenders counter it by making sure something else covers that dead zone.

When you have finished a layout, tap each defence in turn and look at what its circle does not cover. Wherever two circles fail to meet is where the attack will come.

The checklist that catches most bad bases:

  1. Is there splash damage covering the core, and is it centred rather than on the edge?
  2. Is anti-air spread across at least three sides of the base?
  3. Does any single Rage-sized circle contain two or more of your key defences? If so, move one.
  4. Are the highest-value defences inside walls, or are they sitting on the perimeter where cheap troops reach them first?
  5. Is the Clan Castle radius covering the approaches, rather than tucked in a corner?

Then, and this matters more than any checklist, watch your defence replays. The game shows you exactly how you lost. Three replays will tell you more about your base's weakness than any amount of theory. Layout principles are covered in base building principles.

faq.q: What is the difference between splash and single-target defences?
faq.a: Single-target defences shoot one unit at a time for high damage, which suits killing large expensive troops and heroes. Splash defences damage everything in an area for less per hit, which suits killing masses of cheap troops. You need both, because the attacker looks at your base and picks whichever one you are missing.

faq.q: Why do my Air Defences keep dying at once?
faq.a: Almost certainly because they are close enough together to sit under a single spell. Anti-air should be spread across different sides of the base and placed deep, so an attacker has to make a separate effort for each one rather than removing them all with one Rage and a stack of Balloons.

faq.q: Do Mortars have a blind spot?
faq.a: Yes. Mortars have a minimum range and cannot hit units standing directly next to them. Attackers use this on purpose, so make sure another defence covers the ground immediately around each Mortar.

entries.name: Base building principles
entries.h1: Base Building Principles That Actually Hold Up
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Base Building — Principles, Compartments and Layout
entries.description: How to design a Clash of Clans base: compartments, centralised storages, spread anti-air, Clan Castle coverage, and the difference between war, farming and trophy layouts.
entries.blurb: Why copying a layout screenshot rarely works, and what to do instead.
entries.summary: Copied base layouts get you a base that was good against last season's meta, built by someone whose defence levels are not yours. The principles underneath them travel much better. There are perhaps eight of them, and they explain why every good layout looks the way it does.

quick.First question: What is this base for? War, farming, or trophies?
quick.Core idea: Many small compartments, not one big ring
quick.Storages: Are structural, use them as walls

sections.h: Decide what the base is for
sections.body:
The three jobs pull in different directions and no layout does all three well.

  • A farming base protects storages and dark elixir above all else and is entirely willing to give up the Town Hall and the trophies that go with it. If an attacker can take your Town Hall for one star and leave with nothing, you have won that exchange.
  • A trophy base protects the Town Hall above all else, because losing it costs the star and the trophies. Storages can sit further out.
  • A war base protects everything, because war scoring is about total destruction percentage, and it is specifically designed to make three-starring expensive.

Pick one, honestly, based on what you are actually doing this month. A base that half-protects everything protects nothing.

One ring of wall around the whole base is a single door. Break one segment, everything is open. Many small walled cells mean each breach yields one building.

Practical rules:

  • Use storages as compartment walls. They have big hitpoints, they are worth attacking, and every second a troop spends chewing a storage is a second under fire.
  • No double walls. Two segments side by side cost twice as much and break to the same charge. Spend the segments on another compartment.
  • Check for gaps. One missing tile is a free path and pathing finds it instantly. Sweep the whole perimeter after any change.
  • Do not wall single buildings on the outside. A lone walled hut on the perimeter is a wall segment doing nothing.

More on how walls behave in walls and pathing.

• Splash damage goes central. It needs to cover the compartments an attacker must enter, not the edge they can ignore.
  • Anti-air goes wide and deep. Never two Air Defences under one spell radius.
  • The Clan Castle goes central. Its radius should cover every likely approach, so attackers cannot lure it from safety. A corner Castle is a Castle that lures itself.
  • Heroes near the core. Defending heroes are among your best defenders; put their altars where they wake up in time to matter.
  • Traps where troops path, not where you like them. Traps belong on the routes created by your own compartments. Your defence replays show you exactly where troops walk.
  • Keep a tidy perimeter. Spare buildings scattered outside give attackers free funnel work and free percentage.

You cannot evaluate a base by looking at it. You evaluate it by watching it lose.

  1. Play the layout for a few days.Give it enough defences to gather real data rather than one unlucky attack.
  2. Watch every defence replay.Note where the attacker deployed, which compartment fell first, and what killed which troops.
  3. Look for the repeat.If three different attackers all entered from the same side, that side is the problem, not the attackers.
  4. Change one thing.Move one defence or reshape one compartment, then watch again. Changing five things teaches you nothing.

On copied layouts. There is nothing wrong with starting from a good design, but understand that a screenshot is a snapshot of someone else's defence levels against a meta that has moved on. Copy the structure, then adapt it to what you actually have, and iterate from your own replays.

faq.q: Should I protect my Town Hall or my storages?
faq.a: It depends what the base is for. A farming base protects storages and dark elixir and happily gives up the Town Hall, since losing a star costs little compared to losing loot. A trophy base does the opposite. Deciding this first is the most important base building decision.

faq.q: Are copied base layouts a good idea?
faq.a: As a starting point, yes; as a finished answer, no. A copied layout reflects someone else's defence levels and the attack meta at the time it was made. Use the structure, then adapt it and iterate based on your own defence replays.

faq.q: Where should traps go?
faq.a: On the paths your own compartments create, which you find by watching defence replays rather than by guessing. Traps placed where troops actually walk are worth several times traps placed where they look sensible.
