entries.h1: Dark Elixir: The Late-Game Bottleneck
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Dark Elixir — Farming, Drills and What It Is For
entries.description: What dark elixir is used for in Clash of Clans, how drills work, why it becomes the main bottleneck in the late game, and how to farm it efficiently.
entries.blurb: The resource that decides how fast your heroes grow, which is to say everything.
entries.summary: Gold and elixir buy buildings. Dark elixir buys heroes, and heroes are the difference between an army that works and an army that nearly works. From the moment it unlocks, dark elixir is the resource that gates your real progress, and it is the hardest one to get.

quick.Unlocked at: The Town Hall level that introduces the Dark Elixir Drill
quick.Spent on: Heroes, dark troops, dark spells, and some upgrades
quick.Why it is scarce: Drills produce slowly and raids yield small amounts

sections.body:
Dark elixir funds three things, in descending order of importance:

  1. Heroes. The Barbarian King, Archer Queen and their successors are all upgraded with dark elixir, and hero levels contribute to attacking power more than almost any other upgrade in the game. They are also the upgrades with the longest timers, which means every day you are not upgrading a hero is a day permanently lost.
  2. Dark troops. Hog Riders, Valkyries, Witches, Golems and the rest are trained with dark elixir, so a dark-troop army has a running cost as well as a research cost.
  3. Dark spells and assorted upgrades. Cheaper, but they add up.

Because heroes sit at the top of that list and heroes cannot be attacked with while they are upgrading, dark elixir management is really schedule management, which is covered in upgrade priority.

Three reasons compound. Drills produce it far more slowly than mines produce gold. Storages hold a small stealable share, so raiding rich players yields little. And the drills themselves are usually placed inside the base, so you cannot strip them with a surface army the way you strip collectors.

The result is a resource where the difference between a good farming approach and a bad one is enormous. Players who farm dark elixir deliberately upgrade heroes continuously; players who pick it up incidentally spend most of the game with heroes several levels behind.

Three approaches, and most players end up mixing them.

  • Drill sniping. Find bases with drills placed loosely, near the edge or in a poorly defended compartment, and take just the drills with a small cheap force. Fast, cheap, low-yield per attack, high yield per hour if you skip well.
  • Full attacks on storage. Commit a real army to reach the Dark Elixir Storage in the core. Higher yield per attack, much higher cost, and only worth it when the loot preview justifies it.
  • League bonus farming. In higher leagues the bonus includes a meaningful dark elixir component, paid for winning regardless of what you steal. If you win reliably, this is often the most consistent source.

What ties all three together is the skip discipline. Dark elixir farming is a search problem more than a combat problem: set a hard minimum, skip fast, and do not talk yourself into a marginal base because you have been searching for a while.

• Bury the storage. The Dark Elixir Storage belongs in the most protected compartment you have, deeper than gold and elixir.
  • Do not leave drills full. Collect them every time you log in. Dark elixir sitting in a drill is the most stealable dark elixir on your base.
  • Spend it immediately. A hero upgrade in progress cannot be stolen. If you have enough for a hero level, start it before you close the game.

The last point is the one that separates players. Dark elixir left in storage overnight is an invitation; dark elixir committed to a hero is progress you keep.

Drill production rates, capacities and costs for every level are on the Dark Elixir Drill page, read from the game files rather than reproduced here.

faq.q: What is dark elixir used for?
faq.a: Primarily heroes, which are the single biggest contributor to attacking strength, plus dark troops such as Hog Riders and Golems and the dark spells. Because hero upgrades take the longest and matter the most, dark elixir effectively sets the pace of your late-game progress.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to farm dark elixir?
faq.a: Usually drill sniping with a small cheap force combined with a strict skip minimum, since drills hold a large share of stealable dark elixir and are far cheaper to reach than the core storage. In higher leagues the league bonus becomes a large and much more predictable source.

faq.q: Why do I keep losing my dark elixir?
faq.a: Almost always because it is sitting in full drills or in a storage that is not deep enough in the base, or because you logged off holding it. Collect drills every session, keep the Dark Elixir Storage in your most protected compartment, and start a hero upgrade before closing the game.

entries.name: Upgrade priority
entries.h1: Upgrade Priority: What to Build Next
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Upgrade Priority — What to Upgrade First
entries.description: A durable framework for deciding what to upgrade next in Clash of Clans: laboratory first, heroes always, why rushing hurts, and how to keep builders busy.
entries.blurb: One framework that answers the question at every Town Hall level.
entries.summary: The specific answer changes every Town Hall. The framework does not. Keep the laboratory running, keep a hero upgrading, keep every builder busy, and never let the Town Hall run ahead of what is underneath it. Almost every progression mistake in the game is a violation of one of those four.

quick.First priority: Army research and camp capacity, which apply to every attack
quick.Second priority: Defences that cover a whole category, especially anti-air
quick.Cardinal sin: Upgrading the Town Hall before the base under it is ready

sections.h: The four things that should never be idle
sections.body:
Progress in Clash of Clans is measured in parallel timers, not in resources. Resources sitting in a storage do nothing except attract attackers. The four parallel tracks:

  • The laboratory. Research applies to every troop of that type forever, in every future attack. An idle lab is the most expensive idleness in the game.
  • A hero. Hero upgrades take the longest, so the only way to get them done is to always have one running. Yes, that means attacking without that hero for a while. Do it anyway.
  • Every builder. A free builder is a timer you are not running. Even a cheap, low-value upgrade beats an idle builder.
  • The Clan Castle, on defence. Free, and forgotten constantly.

If you check nothing else when you log in, check these.

sections.h: Ordering within a Town Hall level
sections.body:
When you arrive at a new Town Hall, the shopping list is enormous and the temptation is to build the shiny new defence. A more reliable order:

  1. Army camps and barracks. More troops per attack improves every single attack you will make at this Town Hall. This is almost always the highest-value first purchase.
  2. Laboratory, then research. Upgrade the lab early so the research queue can start on the troops you actually use.
  3. Storages. Because if your storages cannot hold the cost of the next upgrade, you physically cannot buy it, and you will spend days confused about why.
  4. Defences that close a category gap. A missing Air Defence is a hole; a fourth Cannon is a decoration. Read defence mechanics for what a category gap looks like.
  5. Everything else.
  6. Walls, continuously, with surplus. Never as a priority, always as a sink.

sections.h: Rushing, and what it actually costs
sections.body:
Rushing means upgrading the Town Hall while the base beneath it is far from complete. It is not forbidden and it is not always wrong, but it is widely misunderstood, so be clear about the trade:

What you gain: access to new buildings, troops and levels sooner.

What you pay: your defences are now several tiers behind the players you meet, so you lose more defences; your army is behind the bases you are offered, so you win fewer attacks; and your war matchups get harder because war matchmaking looks at what you own, not at whether it is upgraded. The result is a village that looks advanced and performs badly, and digging out takes months.

The moderate position most experienced players land on: do not max everything, but do not skip categories. Get heroes, army research, camps and the key defences to a reasonable level for the Town Hall, then move up. Leaving a few decorative buildings behind is fine; leaving your heroes ten levels behind is not.

sections.h: A checklist before pressing Town Hall upgrade
sections.body:
1. Are my heroes within a reasonable range of the cap for this Town Hall?
  2. Is the laboratory maxed for this level, and are the troops I actually use researched?
  3. Are army camps maxed?
  4. Is there a defence category, especially anti-air, that is still weak?
  5. Do I have enough builders free that the next Town Hall's queue will not stall?

Four yeses and a plan for the fifth means go. Two yeses means you are about to rush, and you should know that is what you are doing.

faq.q: What should I upgrade first in Clash of Clans?
faq.a: Army camps and laboratory research before anything else, because they improve every attack you will ever make at that Town Hall level, then storages so you can actually afford later upgrades, then any defence category you are missing. Walls last, always, using surplus.

faq.q: Is rushing your Town Hall bad?
faq.a: It is a trade rather than a mistake. You get access to new content sooner and pay for it with weaker defences, a weaker army relative to your opponents and harder war matchups. The workable middle ground is to keep heroes, research, camps and key defences reasonable for your level, and not worry about maxing decorative buildings.

faq.q: Should I upgrade heroes even though I cannot use them?
faq.a: Yes. Hero upgrades have the longest timers in the game, so the only way to finish them is to always have one running. Attacking without a hero for a few days is a small cost; being permanently behind on hero levels is a large one.

entries.name: Clan Wars
entries.h1: Clan Wars: Scoring, Attacks and Etiquette
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Clan Wars Explained — Stars, Percentages and Strategy
entries.description: How Clan Wars work in Clash of Clans: preparation and battle day, star and percentage scoring, tiebreakers, mirror discipline, and the unwritten rules clans expect you to follow.
entries.blurb: Two attacks, two days, and a scoring system that rewards patience.
entries.summary: Clan Wars are the most structured part of Clash of Clans and the part most new players get quietly wrong, not because the attacks are hard but because the scoring and the etiquette are unfamiliar. Both are learnable in ten minutes and will make you welcome in any decent clan.

quick.Scoring: Stars first, then total destruction percentage as tiebreaker
quick.Stars from a base: Only the best result on that base counts, ever

sections.body:
A clan leader starts a search, matchmaking finds an opposing clan with a comparable roster, and the war enters preparation day. During prep nobody attacks. You set your war base, donate defensive Clan Castle troops to teammates, scout the enemy map and agree who is attacking whom.

Then battle day begins and each member gets two attacks. When the clock runs out, the clan with more stars wins; if stars are level, the clan with the higher total destruction percentage wins.

The single most important scoring rule: only the best result on each enemy base counts. If a teammate already took two stars on base seven and you take two stars as well, your attack contributed nothing. If you take three, you contributed exactly one new star. This is why coordination matters so much more in war than anywhere else in the game.

War maps are ordered by strength, and your position on your map is your mirror, the equivalently ranked base on theirs. Most clans expect you to attack your mirror first, or something close to it, for a simple reason: if everyone attacks down for easy stars, the top of the enemy map never gets touched and the war is lost with a hundred per cent destruction on the bottom half.

The usual convention, which varies by clan:

  • First attack: your mirror, or one or two above it. Try for three stars.
  • Second attack: whatever the clan needs. Late in the war that usually means cleaning up a base sitting on one or two stars, not hunting a fresh three-star for personal satisfaction.
  • Never attack far below your position early. It takes a base out of the pool for the teammate who was meant to handle it, and it wins nothing.

Ask your clan what their convention is. Every clan has one, and being the person who attacked base fourteen from position three is a fast way to be removed from the war roster.

1. Scout before prep ends.Look at your likely targets on preparation day, not thirty seconds before you attack. Note the Clan Castle, the defence layout and the compartments.
  2. Plan the Castle lure.Decide where you will pull the defending Castle and what will kill it. See Clan Castle troops.
  3. Plan the funnel.Pick the side, identify the shoulder buildings you need to clear, decide what clears them. See funnelling.
  4. Request what you need.Castle troops, siege machine, spells. Ask early; donations are not instant.
  5. Attack with time to spare.Do not leave both attacks to the last hour. Clans lose wars to time zones far more often than to skill.

• Use both attacks. An unused attack is a star the clan cannot get. This is the number one reason players are removed from clans.
  • Fill your war base's Clan Castle. An empty war Castle is a free star for the enemy.
  • Do not change your war base mid-war unless your clan asks you to.
  • Call your target in chat before attacking so two people do not burn attacks on the same base.
  • Post the result honestly. If you failed, say what happened; someone else needs to clean it up.

None of this requires skill. All of it makes the difference between a clan that wins wars and a clan that argues about them.

faq.q: How does Clan War scoring work?
faq.a: Stars decide the war, and total destruction percentage breaks a tie. Crucially, only the best result on each enemy base counts, so attacking a base that already has three stars adds nothing at all, and matching a teammate's two stars adds nothing either.

faq.q: Which base should I attack in war?
faq.a: Convention in most clans is to take your mirror, the base at your own position on the enemy map, or one or two above it with your first attack, then use your second attack on whatever the clan still needs. Attacking far below your position early wastes a target another member was meant to handle.

faq.q: What happens if I do not use my war attacks?
faq.a: The clan permanently loses the stars those attacks could have earned, and there is no way to recover them. Unused attacks are the most common reason players are dropped from war rosters or removed from clans entirely.

entries.name: Clan War Leagues
entries.h1: Clan War Leagues: The Monthly Tournament
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Clan War Leagues (CWL) Explained
entries.description: How Clan War Leagues work in Clash of Clans: the seven-war format, one attack per war, promotion and relegation, league medals and roster strategy.
entries.blurb: Seven wars, one attack each, and rewards that dwarf regular war.
entries.summary: Clan War Leagues run once a month as a round-robin tournament between eight clans. The format is different enough from regular war to catch people out, and the rewards are large enough that being caught out is expensive.

quick.Frequency: Once per month, for a limited signup window
quick.Format: Seven consecutive wars against seven different clans
quick.Roster: Fixed size, chosen by leadership, can be rotated between wars
quick.Rewards: League medals, spent in a dedicated shop

sections.body:
In regular war you get two attacks, which means you can afford an experiment and then a clean-up. In Clan War Leagues you get one. There is no second chance, no correcting a bad funnel, no fixing a misjudged Castle lure.

Practical consequences:

  • Take the attack you are confident in, not the attack you have been meaning to practise. CWL is not the place to try a new army for the first time.
  • Scout properly. With one attack, five minutes of scouting is cheap.
  • Clean-up is a team decision. Because nobody has a spare attack, whoever is assigned a base has to finish it. Communication matters even more than in regular war.

Clans are placed in a league tier and play seven wars. Performance across those wars decides whether the clan is promoted, held or relegated for next season, and the tier determines how many medals everyone earns.

Because the roster is a fixed size and leadership chooses it per war, CWL creates a genuine selection problem. Two common approaches:

  • Compete: field the strongest available roster every war, prioritise promotion, accept that weaker members sit out some wars.
  • Rotate: give everyone participation across the seven wars so all members earn medals, accept a lower finish.

Neither is wrong, but a clan that has not decided which one it is doing will have an argument about it in week two. If you are joining a clan for CWL, ask which it is before signing up.

League medals are earned based on the clan's tier and your own participation, and are spent in a dedicated shop that typically stocks hero-relevant items, resources and boosts.

The general spending advice: buy the things that are otherwise scarce. Resources you can farm. Time you cannot. Items that shorten hero upgrades or advance research are worth more than an equivalent value in gold, because your bottleneck is almost never gold, it is the timers described in upgrade priority.

faq.q: How many attacks do you get in Clan War Leagues?
faq.a: One per war, across seven wars. That is the key difference from regular Clan Wars, where you get two, and it means CWL attacks should be conservative and well scouted rather than experimental.

faq.q: Do I have to participate in every CWL war?
faq.a: No. Leadership picks the roster for each of the seven wars and can rotate members between them. Whether your clan rotates everyone through for medals or fields its strongest roster to chase promotion is a clan policy decision worth asking about before you sign up.

faq.q: What should I spend league medals on?
faq.a: Items that save time rather than items that save resources. Resources can be farmed; hero and research timers cannot be, so anything that shortens them is worth more than its face value in gold or elixir.

entries.name: Clan Capital and Raid Weekends
entries.h1: Clan Capital and Raid Weekends
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Clan Capital and Raid Weekends
entries.description: How the Clan Capital works in Clash of Clans: capital gold, districts, contributing to upgrades, Raid Weekend attack mechanics and raid medals.
entries.blurb: A second, shared village that the whole clan builds together.
entries.summary: The Clan Capital is a separate, collectively owned village made of districts, funded by capital gold that every member contributes. Raid Weekends are the attack mode built on top of it, and they run on rules that are unlike anything else in the game.

quick.Currency: Capital gold, which cannot be converted to or from village resources
quick.Structure: A capital peak plus unlockable districts
quick.Raid Weekend: A weekend event where clans attack other clans' capitals
quick.Rewards: Raid medals, spent in a dedicated shop

sections.body:
Capital gold is earned separately from your village economy and can only be spent on the Clan Capital. You cannot convert village gold into capital gold or the other way round, which means capital progress is genuinely a collective effort rather than something one rich member can carry.

Members contribute capital gold to specific upgrades, and upgrades complete when enough has been contributed. Two things worth knowing:

  • Contribute where leadership asks. Spreading contributions across every building at once means nothing finishes. Most clans nominate a target.
  • Do not sit on capital gold. It has no other use. Hoarding it helps nobody, including you.

Raid Weekends run on rules that catch out everyone who assumes they work like village attacks:

  • Damage carries over. If your attack does not finish a district but destroys most of it, the destruction persists for the next attacker. Attacks are cumulative, not independent.
  • Troops do not return. You get a limited number of attacks, and each one uses one of them regardless of how it goes.
  • Districts unlock in sequence. You must clear one district to reach the next, so the clan works through the enemy capital in order.
  • Everything is shared. Your attacks feed a clan-wide result, and the clan's total performance decides the reward.

The carry-over rule is the important one strategically. A partial attack is not a wasted attack; it is groundwork. Clans coordinate by sending strong attackers to open a district and everyone else to finish it.

Raid medals are awarded based on the clan's raid performance and your own participation, and are spent in a shop that typically includes resources, boosts and items relevant to hero and research progress.

The same principle as league medals applies: buy time, not resources. A shop item that shortens a hero upgrade is worth considerably more than the equivalent in gold, because gold is the thing you can always go and get.

The practical advice for members is simply to use every raid attack, every weekend. Raid medals are one of the steadiest reward streams in the game and they cost you nothing but a few minutes.

faq.q: Can I convert capital gold into normal gold?
faq.a: No. Capital gold is a separate currency that can only be spent on Clan Capital upgrades, and village resources cannot be converted into it either. That separation is deliberate, so capital progress reflects collective participation rather than one wealthy member.

faq.q: Does damage carry over between Raid Weekend attacks?
faq.a: Yes, and this is the most important rule in the mode. Destruction persists for the next attacker, so a partial attack is groundwork rather than a failure. Clans coordinate by having strong attackers open a district and others finish it.

faq.q: What should I buy with raid medals?
faq.a: Items that shorten upgrade and research timers, rather than raw resources. Resources can be farmed at any time; the timers on heroes and laboratory research are the real constraint on progress.

entries.name: War weight
entries.h1: War Weight: What It Is and What It Is Not
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans War Weight Explained — Myths and Reality
entries.description: What war weight means in Clash of Clans, how war matchmaking really evaluates a roster, why engineered bases stopped working, and what clans should actually do.
entries.blurb: The most misunderstood number in the game, and mostly a distraction.
entries.summary: War weight is the informal name for how war matchmaking evaluates your village. It generated years of folklore, elaborate spreadsheets and a whole culture of engineered bases. Most of that folklore was already out of date when it was written, and almost none of it is worth your time now.

quick.What it measures: Roughly, the offensive and defensive assets a village owns
quick.Based on: What you have built and upgraded, not on trophies
quick.Applies to: Clan War and Clan War League matchmaking
quick.Practical advice: Build a balanced village and stop optimising for it

sections.body:
When a clan searches for a war, matchmaking evaluates the participating rosters and looks for an opposing clan of comparable strength. It considers what each village has built and upgraded, offensive assets as well as defensive ones. That evaluation is what players call war weight. Supercell has never published the formula and has changed it repeatedly.

The important part, and the part that overturns most of the old folklore: offence counts. In early versions of the game, matchmaking leaned heavily on defensive buildings, which created a well-known exploit.

sections.h: Engineered bases, and why they died
sections.body:
The exploit was the engineered or anti-3-star account: a village that deliberately skipped defensive upgrades while maxing offence, so it would be weighted low, placed near the bottom of the war map, and could then attack far above its apparent level. A clan full of these could consistently out-punch its matchups.

Supercell addressed this over several years by giving offensive assets real weight in matchmaking and by adjusting how war maps are ordered. The result is that engineering now mostly produces the opposite of what it was designed to produce: a village that is weighted according to its strong offence and matched accordingly, but that defends like a much lower Town Hall, so it hands out easy stars all war.

You will still meet players insisting otherwise, generally quoting advice that was accurate around a decade ago.

Three pieces of advice that survive every matchmaking change:

  • Build balanced villages. A village whose offence and defence roughly match its Town Hall matches fairly and performs where it is placed. This is the whole answer.
  • Manage the roster, not the weight. The lever a clan genuinely controls is who participates. Fielding fifteen committed attackers beats fielding thirty of whom half forget.
  • Stop worrying about the number. Time spent modelling war weight is time not spent upgrading heroes, and hero levels win wars.

A note on the folklore. Much of the war weight content online, including detailed per-building weight tables, dates from an era with a different formula. Treat any specific number you find as historical unless it is very recent and sourced.

faq.q: Does upgrading defences make my war matchups harder?
faq.a: It contributes, but so does upgrading your army, heroes and laboratory, because modern war matchmaking weighs offensive assets as well as defensive ones. Deliberately skipping defences no longer buys you an easy matchup; it just makes you easier to three-star.

faq.q: Do engineered bases still work?
faq.a: Not in the way they were designed to. Once offensive assets started counting toward matchmaking, an account with maxed offence and neglected defence gets weighted for its offence and then loses defences all war. The strategy is a relic of a much older version of the game.

faq.q: Do trophies affect war matchmaking?
faq.a: No. War matchmaking evaluates the participating rosters' assets and ignores trophies entirely, which is why trophy dropping has no effect on the wars your clan is matched into.

entries.name: Builder Base
entries.h1: Builder Base: The Second Village
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Builder Base Explained
entries.description: How the Builder Base works in Clash of Clans: Builder Hall progression, versus battle rules, the separate economy, and how it feeds your main village.
entries.blurb: A separate village with its own economy, its own troops and its own rules.
entries.summary: The Builder Base is a parallel game. It has its own resources, its own troops, its own attack mode and its own progression, and it feeds back into the main village through the rewards it produces. Many players ignore it, which is a mistake, because it is the least demanding source of steady progress in the game.

quick.Unlocked by: Repairing the boat, after a certain main village Town Hall level
quick.Progression building: Builder Hall, rather than Town Hall
quick.Economy: Separate gold and elixir that cannot be moved to the main village
quick.Attack mode: Versus battles against another player's base
quick.Feeds back: Through rewards that benefit the main village

sections.body:
Versus battles are not raids. You and an opponent attack the same layout, and the better result wins. The differences from main village attacking are substantial:

  • You are not stealing. There is no loot on the defender's base to take. Rewards come from winning, not from what you destroy.
  • Troops are automatic between waves. The Builder Base has its own troop roster with its own behaviours and its own deployment rhythm.
  • Both sides see the same base. It is a comparison, not a raid, so a marginal result is only bad if your opponent did better.
  • Attacks are limited per day for full rewards. This is the important one economically, and it shapes how you should play.

Because full rewards come from a limited number of attacks per day, the Builder Base rewards consistency over volume. A player who takes their handful of attacks every day progresses steadily; a player who does thirty attacks on Saturday and none all week gets far less for far more effort.

The efficient routine is short:

  1. Log in, collect the mines and the Gem Mine.
  2. Take your rewarded attacks, in one sitting, with whatever army you have researched.
  3. Start upgrades with everything you earned.
  4. Close the game.

Five minutes a day, and over a month it is a meaningful amount of progress that costs you almost no attention. If you want that loop run for you, that is exactly what a Builder Base bot does.

sections.h: What it gives the main village
sections.body:
The Builder Base is not a closed system. Progress there unlocks rewards that matter on the main village, most notably additional building capacity and various items and boosts that feed main village progress. That is the real argument for taking it seriously: it is not a side game, it is a second income stream for the village you actually care about.

The practical implication for upgrade order is that Builder Hall progression is worth prioritising early, because the rewards it unlocks compound over the entire rest of your account's life. A player who reaches those milestones in month two benefits from them for years.

faq.q: Can I move resources between the Builder Base and my main village?
faq.a: No. The two villages have entirely separate economies, and Builder Base gold and elixir can only be spent on Builder Base upgrades. The connection between them is through the rewards and unlocks that Builder Hall progression grants to the main village.

faq.q: Is the Builder Base worth playing?
faq.a: Yes, mainly because of what it unlocks for the main village, including additional building capacity. It also asks very little: a handful of rewarded attacks a day, taken consistently, produces steady progress for around five minutes of attention.

faq.q: How many versus battles should I do per day?
faq.a: Enough to claim the full daily rewards, and consistency matters far more than volume. Attacks beyond the rewarded ones give much less, so a short daily session beats a long weekend one.

entries.name: Super Troops
entries.h1: Super Troops: Temporary Upgrades
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Super Troops Explained — Boosting, Cost and Strategy
entries.description: How Super Troops work in Clash of Clans: boosting with dark elixir, the active duration, how many you can run at once, and whether they are worth the cost.
entries.blurb: A temporary, much stronger version of a troop you already have.
entries.summary: Super Troops are enhanced versions of standard troops, activated for a limited period by spending dark elixir. While active, the boosted troop replaces its normal counterpart entirely. They are genuinely powerful, genuinely expensive, and worth activating with a plan rather than on impulse.

quick.Requirement: The base troop must be at a minimum level
quick.Cost: Dark elixir, or a Super Potion
quick.Duration: A fixed active period, measured in days
quick.Limit: A small number active at once

sections.body:
You pick a troop that meets the level requirement, pay dark elixir, and for a fixed period that troop is replaced in your army menu by its Super version. You cannot train both the normal and the Super version at the same time, which is the detail that catches people out: boosting a troop your farming army depends on changes that army's cost and housing for the whole boost period.

Only a small number can be active simultaneously, so activation is a choice between options rather than a shopping spree.

sections.h: Is it worth the dark elixir?
sections.body:
Dark elixir is the scarcest resource in the game and its main competing use is hero upgrades, which are the single biggest contributor to attacking power. So the honest framing is: a Super Troop boost costs you hero progress.

That makes it worth it in a narrow set of cases:

  • You have a specific war coming and the Super version solves a problem your normal army cannot.
  • The boost dramatically improves your farming rate, such that it pays for itself in dark elixir over the boost period. Do the arithmetic rather than assuming.
  • You got a Super Potion from an event or the shop, in which case it costs nothing and you should absolutely use it.

It is generally not worth it if you are mid-hero-upgrade and short on dark elixir, or if you are boosting a troop you do not have a specific plan for. See dark elixir for the wider budgeting picture.

Because the duration is fixed and the cost is high, the boost should be planned around what you will do with it:

  1. Decide the job first.War attacks, dark elixir farming, or a push. Different jobs favour different Super Troops.
  2. Check your army still works.The Super version usually has different housing space, so your existing army composition may not fit any more. Rebuild it before you activate, not after.
  3. Activate at the start of the window.Boosting on the last day of a war wastes most of the duration.
  4. Use it every day it is active.An unused boost is dark elixir set on fire.

faq.q: Are Super Troops worth the dark elixir?
faq.a: Only with a specific plan. Dark elixir competes directly with hero upgrades, which contribute more to attacking power over time, so a boost is worth it when it solves a concrete problem for an upcoming war or clearly pays for itself in improved farming. Free Super Potions are always worth using.

faq.q: Can I use the normal troop while its Super version is active?
faq.a: No. The Super version replaces the standard troop in your army menu for the entire boost duration, and since housing space usually differs, your existing army composition may no longer fit. Rebuild the army before activating.

faq.q: How many Super Troops can I have active at once?
faq.a: Only a small number, so activation is a genuine choice between options rather than something you do to everything at once. Pick based on what you actually intend to attack during the boost window.

entries.name: Hero Equipment
entries.h1: Hero Equipment: Customising Your Heroes
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Hero Equipment Explained — Slots, Upgrades and Choices
entries.description: How Hero Equipment works in Clash of Clans: equipment slots, ores and upgrading, choosing between offensive and defensive pieces, and what changes on defence.
entries.blurb: Two slots per hero that change what the hero is for.
entries.summary: Hero Equipment turned heroes from fixed units into configurable ones. Each hero carries a small number of equipment pieces, each piece changes their abilities and passive strengths, and the combination you choose can make the same hero a tank, a damage dealer or a support unit.

quick.Slots: A small fixed number per hero
quick.Upgraded with: Ores, a separate currency from resources
quick.Swappable: Yes, between attacks, at no cost

sections.body:
Each hero has a small number of equipment slots, and the pieces you fit determine both the hero's ability and a set of passive bonuses. Swapping is free and can be done between attacks, which means equipment is a per-attack decision, not a permanent commitment.

This is the part people underuse. Most players find one loadout and never touch it again. The players who get the most out of equipment change it for the job: one setup for farming, another for war, another for defence.

Equipment is upgraded with ores, which are earned through play rather than farmed like gold, and the rarer ores are genuinely scarce. That scarcity creates the central decision: spread ores thinly across many pieces, or concentrate them on a few.

Concentrating is almost always correct. A small number of high-level pieces on the heroes you actually attack with beats a broad shelf of mediocre equipment, because you can only equip a few pieces at a time anyway. Pick the loadout you use most, level it properly, and ignore the rest until it is done.

  • Prioritise the hero you use every attack. Equipment on a hero you rarely deploy is wasted.
  • Prioritise offence over defence pieces unless you are actively pushing trophies, because attacks are where your resources come from.
  • Do not chase every new release. New equipment is added regularly; ores are not.

Defending heroes use their equipment too, which means the loadout you left on before logging off is the loadout defending your base. If you have configured a hero purely for offensive burst and then log out, you are defending with that configuration.

Whether that matters depends on what your base is for. A trophy pusher should think about it; a farmer who keeps empty storages and welcomes shields largely should not. But it is worth knowing that the choice exists, because it is invisible in the interface and surprises people when they finally notice it.

faq.q: Can I change Hero Equipment between attacks?
faq.a: Yes, freely and at no cost. Equipment is a per-attack decision, so it is worth keeping a farming loadout and a war loadout and switching between them rather than settling on one configuration permanently.

faq.q: Should I spread ores across all my equipment?
faq.a: No. Concentrate them on the few pieces you actually equip on the heroes you actually attack with. You can only use a small number of pieces at a time, so a handful of well-levelled pieces beats a large collection of weak ones.

faq.q: Does Hero Equipment affect defending heroes?
faq.a: Yes. Whatever loadout is equipped when you log off is what your defending heroes use, which matters if you are pushing trophies and matters much less if you are farming with empty storages.

entries.name: Magic items
entries.h1: Magic Items: Books, Runes, Potions and Hammers
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Magic Items — Books, Hammers and Runes
entries.description: What Clash of Clans magic items do: Books of Building and Heroes, Hammers, Runes and Potions, where they come from, and how to use them without wasting them.
entries.blurb: Finite time-savers. Spend them on the longest timer you have.
entries.summary: Magic items skip or accelerate the thing the game is actually made of, which is waiting. They are finite, they do not expire, and the single most common mistake players make is using them on a small upgrade because it was convenient at the time.

quick.Sources: Season Challenges, Clan Games, league and raid shops, events
quick.Expire: No, they sit in storage indefinitely
quick.Books: Instantly complete one upgrade of a given type
quick.Hammers: Instantly complete and pay for an upgrade
quick.Potions: Temporarily boost a system, such as training or research

sections.body:
Spend a magic item on the longest timer you can. That is essentially the whole strategy, and it is violated constantly.

A Book of Heroes used on a two-day hero upgrade saved you two days. The same book used on a fourteen-day one saved you fourteen. The book cost the same. Since books do not expire, holding one for three weeks until a big upgrade unlocks costs you nothing and multiplies its value several times over.

The same logic applies to hammers, which are rarer still and should be reserved for the most expensive, longest upgrade available to you at your current Town Hall.

• Books instantly finish one upgrade of a matching type: building, hero, fighting, or spell. They do not pay for it, so you still need the resources in the bank first.
  • Hammers instantly finish and pay for an upgrade. They are the rarest items in the game and should be treated accordingly.
  • Runes instantly fill a resource storage to capacity. Their value therefore scales with your storage level, which means a rune used at a low Town Hall is worth a fraction of the same rune used later. Hold them.
  • Potions temporarily boost a system: training speed, research speed, builder speed, clock speed. Best used at the start of a session where you will actually exploit the boost, not tapped at random.

• Do not tap items to clear a notification. The red dot is not a reason.
  • Check the timer before spending. If the upgrade is under a day, it is almost never the right target.
  • Runes get better the longer you hold them. Since they fill storages to capacity and storage capacity grows, an unspent rune is an appreciating asset.
  • Potions want a plan. A training potion is worth using when you have an hour to farm, not when you are about to log off.
  • Save around Town Hall transitions. The upgrades immediately after a Town Hall jump are the longest and most expensive ones you will meet, and that is exactly when your saved items pay out most.

How magic items fit the broader schedule is covered in upgrade priority.

faq.q: When should I use a Book of Heroes?
faq.a: On the longest hero upgrade available to you, not on whatever is running now. Books do not expire, so holding one until a fourteen-day upgrade unlocks is strictly better than spending it on a two-day one, and it costs you nothing to wait.

faq.q: Do magic items expire?
faq.a: No. They sit in your storage indefinitely, which is exactly why hoarding them until a high-value moment, typically just after a Town Hall upgrade, is the correct strategy.

faq.q: What is the best use of a Rune of Gold or Elixir?
faq.a: Later rather than sooner. A rune fills your storages to capacity, so its value grows as your storage capacity grows. Using one at a low Town Hall wastes most of its potential.

entries.name: Season Challenges and the Gold Pass
entries.h1: Season Challenges and the Gold Pass
entries.head_title: Clash of Clans Season Challenges and Gold Pass
entries.description: How Season Challenges work in Clash of Clans, what the Gold Pass adds, whether it is worth buying, and how to complete the season efficiently.
entries.blurb: A monthly reward track, and the one purchase most players consider.
entries.summary: Season Challenges are a monthly track of tasks that pay out magic items, resources and cosmetics. The Gold Pass is a paid upgrade to that track which adds rewards and quality-of-life boosts. It is the game's central monetisation, and it is worth understanding clearly rather than defensively.

quick.Gold Pass: Paid upgrade, adds rewards and boosts
quick.Typical rewards: Magic items, resources, hero skins and cosmetics
quick.Key boost: Reduced upgrade costs and times while active

sections.body:
Each month presents a list of challenges, from trivial to substantial. Completing them earns season points, and points unlock tiers on a reward track. The free track pays out meaningfully on its own; the paid track pays out more and adds boosts that apply while the season is active.

Two mechanical points that matter:

  • Challenges are not all worth the same. Some are completed incidentally while playing normally; others demand a specific effort. Sort by points per effort, not by order in the list.
  • The clock is the constraint. The month is the limit, so pacing matters more than intensity. Most of a season is finished by simply playing normally.

sections.h: Is the Gold Pass worth buying?
sections.body:
Honest answer: it depends almost entirely on whether you are actively upgrading.

Worth it if you play most days, have builders running constantly, and are in the middle of a Town Hall's worth of expensive upgrades. The cost and time reductions apply to everything you build during the month, and for an active player they compound into a substantial saving. The magic items alone are frequently worth more than the price to someone using them well.

Not worth it if you play occasionally, have builders sitting idle, or are between projects. The boosts only pay out on activity, so buying a pass and then not playing is simply spending money.

This is not a subscription trap in the usual sense, in that nothing is taken away when you stop buying. It is a discount on activity you were already doing. Whether it is a good discount depends on how much activity there is.

1. Read the list at the start of the month and note which challenges need a specific effort, such as using a particular troop or attacking a particular way.
  2. Batch the awkward ones. If three challenges want the same troop, do them in one sitting rather than three.
  3. Do not distort your farming for small challenges. A challenge worth a few points is not worth wrecking a week of loot efficiency.
  4. Bank the magic items. Season rewards are the main source of books and hammers for most players, and they should go straight into storage until a long timer appears. See magic items.

faq.q: Is the Gold Pass worth it in Clash of Clans?
faq.a: For an active player with builders constantly busy, generally yes, because the cost and time reductions apply to every upgrade during the month and the magic items alone often exceed the price in practical value. For someone playing occasionally with idle builders, no, since the benefits only pay out on activity.

faq.q: Can I complete Season Challenges without the Gold Pass?
faq.a: Yes. The free track is available to everyone and pays out real rewards including magic items. The Gold Pass adds to that track rather than gating it.

faq.q: What should I do with season reward magic items?
faq.a: Store them rather than spending them immediately. Season rewards are most players' main supply of books and hammers, and their value multiplies when saved for the long upgrades that appear just after a Town Hall jump.
